results.title: Difference Between Softplus and Softmax Activation Functions
results.content: # Difference Between Softplus and Softmax Activation Functions. Softplus and Softmax are both activation functions used in neural networks, but they serve very different purposes. ### 1️⃣ Softplus Activation Function. The Softplus function is a smooth approximation of the ReLU function, used in regression and some deep learning applications. ✅ Range: (0,∞) Always positive, never negative) ✅ Use Case: Used when output values must be positive (e.g., modeling positive values like variance in Gaussian distributions). ✅ Derivative: The derivative of Softplus is the Sigmoid function:. * For large x, Softplus behaves like x (linear behavior similar to ReLU). ✅ Alternative to ReLU: Unlike ReLU, Softplus is smooth and differentiable everywhere. * Used in Gaussian-based models (e.g., Variational Autoencoders, probabilistic deep learning). The Softmax function is used in classification tasks, especially for multi-class classification. For an input vector z=(z1,z2,...,zn) the Softmax function converts each zi into a probability:. ✅ Range: (0,1) for each class (All values sum to 1, making them interpretable as probabilities). ✅ Use Case: Used for multi-class classification (e.g., predicting categories like "cat," "dog," "bird"). * Used for multi-class problems where each output represents a class probability. ### Softplus → Used for continuous and positive-valued outputs, acts as a smooth ReLU. ### Softmax → Used for multi-class classification, converts outputs into probabilities. results.title: Summary of — SegNet: A Deep Convolutional Encoder-Decoder Architecture for Image Segmentation | by Siddhant Kumar | TDS Archive | Medium
results.content: ## TDS Archive. # Summary of — SegNet: A Deep Convolutional Encoder-Decoder Architecture for Image Segmentation. * Uses a novel technique to upsample encoder output which involves storing the max-pooling indices used in pooling layer. * Semantic pixel-wise labelling i.e. labelling each pixel of an image to belong to some class(tree, road, sky, etc) as shown in the image. Direct adoption of classification networks for pixel wise segmentation yields poor results mainly because *max-pooling* and *subsampling* reduce feature map resolution and hence output resolution is reduced. * Trained on road scene datasets hence, classes represent macro objects, hence segmentations are desired to be smooth. ## SegNet- Architecture. Encoder-Decoder pairs are used to create feature maps for classifications of different resolutions. ## Encoder. Each encoder is like Fig 3. The novelty is in the subsampling stage, Max-pooling is used to achieve translation invariance over small spatial shifts in the image, combine that with Subsampling and it leads to each pixel governing a *larger input image context* (spatial window). These methods achieve better classification accuracy but reduce the feature map size, this leads to lossy image representation with blurred boundaries which is not ideal for segmentation purpose. It is desired that output image resolution is same as input image, to achieve this SegNet does Upsampling in its decoder, to do that it needs to store some information. It is necessary to *capture and store* boundary information in the encoder feature maps before sub-sampling. In order to to that space efficiently, SegNet stores only the *max-pooling indices* i.e. the locations of maximum feature value in each pooling window is memorised for each encoder map. This form of upsampling can be incorporated in any encoder-decoder architecture. ## Decoder. * For each of the 13 encoders there is a corresponding decoder which upsamples the feature map using memorised *max-pooling indices*. * Sparse feature maps of higher resolutions produced. * Sparse maps are fed through a *trainable filter bank* to produce dense feature maps. * The last decoder is connected to a *softmax classifier* which classifies each pixel. SegNet paper compares its technique with several other decoders as shown in Fig 5. ## Published in TDS Archive.
